content: The document titled Web Annex F: Consolidated Guidelines on HIV Testing Services, 2019 focuses on modeling the cost-effectiveness of maternal HIV retesting in settings with high and low HIV burdens. It was authored by Julianne Meisner, Allen Roberts, Patricia Rodriguez, Morkor Newman Owiredu, Monisha Sharma, Bertha Gomez, and others, and published by the World Health Organization (WHO) in 2020. 1. Background: Retesting for HIV during late pregnancy and breastfeeding is critical for identifying new maternal infections and preventing mother-to-child transmission (MTCT) of HIV. However, the optimal timing and cost-effectiveness of such retesting remain uncertain. 2. Methods: The study utilized Markov models to evaluate the health and economic impacts of maternal HIV retesting on MTCT in four countries: Kenya and South Africa (high/intermediate HIV prevalence) and Colombia and Ukraine (low HIV prevalence). Five retesting scenarios were assessed, varying in frequency from late pregnancy through nine months postpartum. Strategies were compared using incremental cost-effectiveness ratios (ICERs) against a cost-effectiveness threshold of 50% of the gross domestic product (GDP). 3. Findings: In Kenya and South Africa, retesting once during late pregnancy with follow-up testing through six weeks postpartum was cost-effective. It prevented 24% and 21% of infant HIV infections attributable to new maternal infections, respectively, with ICERs of $241 per disability-adjusted life year (DALY) averted in Kenya and $572 in South Africa. Adding one or two additional retests during the postpartum period provided marginal benefits, reducing infections by an additional 2–4%. However, adding three retests during the postpartum period resulted in higher benefits (5–8% more infections averted) but exceeded the cost-effectiveness threshold, with ICERs of $7,820 in Kenya and $10,463 in South Africa. In Colombia and Ukraine, all retesting strategies exceeded the cost-effectiveness threshold and prevented only a small number of infant infections (up to 33 in Colombia and 5 in Ukraine). This was due to the low HIV prevalence and low breastfeeding rates among HIV-positive mothers in these countries. 4. Interpretation: In high HIV burden settings, retesting once during late pregnancy is the most cost-effective strategy for preventing infant HIV infections. Adding one or two postpartum tests marginally reduced MTCT and was less costly than adding three retests. In low HIV burden settings like Colombia and Ukraine, retesting was not cost-effective at any time point due to the low prevalence of HIV and breastfeeding rates. 5. General Notes: The publication is part of the WHO's consolidated guidelines on HIV testing services and is made publicly available for transparency and informational purposes. The WHO emphasizes that the views expressed in the publication are those of the named authors and do not necessarily represent the organization's official stance. The document includes disclaimers regarding the use of WHO's logo, copyright, and liability for the interpretation and use of the material. 6. Data Summary: The study provides detailed data on infant HIV infections, deaths averted, total costs, incremental costs, DALYs averted, and ICERs for each retesting scenario in the four countries. Late antenatal care (ANC) retesting, defined as testing between 36–39 weeks of gestation, was the most effective and cost-efficient strategy in high HIV burden settings. Scenarios involving frequent postpartum retesting (e.g., every three months) were less cost-effective due to higher incremental costs and limited additional benefits. This publication underscores the importance of tailoring HIV retesting strategies to the epidemiological context of each country, balancing cost-effectiveness with the potential to reduce MTCT.
